1	## Related Work
2	
3	**Safe Robot Learning.**
4	Ensuring collision-free behavior in learned robot policies has been approached primarily through inference-time interventions.
5	One category embeds safety constraints directly into generative processes: SafeDiffuser (Xiao et al., 2025) incorporates CBF invariance into each diffusion denoising step, providing adaptable safety---constraints can be swapped by changing the CBF without retraining---at the cost of per-step barrier computation that scales with the denoising horizon, while OmniGuide (Song et al., 2026) applies differentiable SDF-based energy fields to guide flow-matching VLAs, improving collision avoidance from 7.0% to 93.5% CAR on RoboCasa at the cost of approximately 2$\times$ inference latency.
6	A second category applies reactive post-hoc corrections: AEGIS/VLSA (Hu et al., 2025) projects VLA actions into CBF-certified safe regions, achieving strong results on SafeLIBERO (68.13% TSR, 77.85% CAR on $\pi_{0.5}$), but such generate-then-correct pipelines produce jerky trajectories from hard constraint projections and risk compounding errors as corrected actions push the policy into out-of-distribution states where subsequent predictions degrade---a failure mode the authors themselves acknowledge. These reactive approaches offer robustness to novel obstacles through real-time geometric checks, but at the cost of latency and trajectory naturalness that proactive internalization avoids.
7	Training-time approaches have also been explored, primarily through constrained RL: building on state-wise constrained policy optimization foundations (SCPO; Zhao et al., 2024), SafeVLA (Zhang et al., 2025) reduces cumulative safety cost by 83.58\% via constrained policy optimization. While constrained RL can encode multi-step safety objectives that single-step geometric supervision cannot, these methods require reward shaping and iterative policy-constraint optimization loops that add substantial training complexity, and their abstract cost functions lack the geometric grounding for precise spatial collision reasoning. CoFreeVLA (2026) trains a binary risk estimator for dual-arm collision gating without continuous geometric shaping.
8	Across these paradigms, a tension persists: inference-time methods add latency and risk OOD drift or local minima in dense clutter, while training-time RL methods lack the geometric structure for precise spatial collision reasoning.
9	GeoSafe resolves this tension by internalizing SDF collision geometry into VLA weights during training, producing inherently safe actions with zero inference overhead.
10	
11	**Vision-Language-Action Models.**
12	The development of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has progressed from diffusion-based action generation to flow-matching architectures with broad generalization.
13	$\pi_0$ (Black et al., 2024) introduced a flow-matching VLA built on PaliGemma, pre-trained across eight robot platforms on over 10,000 hours of demonstration data, and established the foundation for general-purpose robot control via flow matching.
14	Its successor $\pi_{0.5}$ (Black et al., 2025) extends this framework to open-world generalization through co-training on heterogeneous tasks, with open-source weights and fine-tuning infrastructure via the openpi codebase.
15	Recent work has explored incorporating geometric priors into these architectures.

## Related Work

**Safe Robot Learning.**
Ensuring collision-free behavior in learned robot policies has been approached primarily through inference-time interventions.
One category embeds safety constraints directly into generative processes: SafeDiffuser (Xiao et al., 2025) incorporates CBF invariance into each diffusion denoising step, providing adaptable safety---constraints can be swapped by changing the CBF without retraining---at the cost of per-step barrier computation that scales with the denoising horizon, while OmniGuide (Song et al., 2026) applies differentiable SDF-based energy fields to guide flow-matching VLAs, improving collision avoidance from 7.0% to 93.5% CAR on RoboCasa at the cost of approximately 2$\times$ inference latency.
A second category applies reactive post-hoc corrections: AEGIS/VLSA (Hu et al., 2025) projects VLA actions into CBF-certified safe regions, achieving strong results on SafeLIBERO (68.13% TSR, 77.85% CAR on $\pi_{0.5}$), but such generate-then-correct pipelines produce jerky trajectories from hard constraint projections and risk compounding errors as corrected actions push the policy into out-of-distribution states where subsequent predictions degrade---a failure mode the authors themselves acknowledge. These reactive approaches offer robustness to novel obstacles through real-time geometric checks, but at the cost of latency and trajectory naturalness that proactive internalization avoids.
Training-time approaches have also been explored, primarily through constrained RL: building on state-wise constrained policy optimization foundations (SCPO; Zhao et al., 2024), SafeVLA (Zhang et al., 2025) reduces cumulative safety cost by 83.58\% via constrained policy optimization. While constrained RL can encode multi-step safety objectives that single-step geometric supervision cannot, these methods require reward shaping and iterative policy-constraint optimization loops that add substantial training complexity, and their abstract cost functions lack the geometric grounding for precise spatial collision reasoning. CoFreeVLA (2026) trains a binary risk estimator for dual-arm collision gating without continuous geometric shaping.
Across these paradigms, a tension persists: inference-time methods add latency and risk OOD drift or local minima in dense clutter, while training-time RL methods lack the geometric structure for precise spatial collision reasoning.
GeoSafe resolves this tension by internalizing SDF collision geometry into VLA weights during training, producing inherently safe actions with zero inference overhead.

**Vision-Language-Action Models.**
The development of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has progressed from diffusion-based action generation to flow-matching architectures with broad generalization.
$\pi_0$ (Black et al., 2024) introduced a flow-matching VLA built on PaliGemma, pre-trained across eight robot platforms on over 10,000 hours of demonstration data, and established the foundation for general-purpose robot control via flow matching.
Its successor $\pi_{0.5}$ (Black et al., 2025) extends this framework to open-world generalization through co-training on heterogeneous tasks, with open-source weights and fine-tuning infrastructure via the openpi codebase.
Recent work has explored incorporating geometric priors into these architectures.

GeoSafe specializes the "train-with, infer-without" approach to collision avoidance: rather than general spatial alignment, we internalize configuration-space SDF into the policy network through an auxiliary loss that directly shapes flow-matching velocity fields away from obstacle boundaries.

The concept of internalizing inference-time guidance into model weights originates in image generation.
Meng et al. (2023) showed that classifier-free guidance in diffusion models can be distilled through a two-step process, enabling high-fidelity generation in 1--4 steps with 10$\times$ acceleration, and proved that guidance can reside in weights rather than requiring runtime computation.
GeoSafe adapts this paradigm to VLA safety: instead of distilling classifier-free guidance for image quality, we internalize SDF collision guidance into flow-matching velocity fields for safe action generation.
Rather than distilling guided sampling trajectories into a student network, we directly shape the velocity field through an SDF auxiliary head whose gradients penalize collision-prone flow vectors during training, and drop this head entirely at inference.

6	### 3.1 Problem Formulation
7	
8	**Flow-matching action generation.** $\pi_{0.5}$ generates robot action trajectories through conditional flow matching. Given an observation $o$ (RGB images and a language instruction), the model learns a velocity field $v_\theta(x_t, o, t)$ that transports samples from a noise distribution to the data distribution of action chunks. Let $a \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times D_a}$ denote a ground-truth action chunk of horizon $H$ and dimension $D_a$, and let $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ be Gaussian noise. 9	
10	$$x_t = (1 - t) \, a + t \, \epsilon,$$
11	
12	where $t = 0$ corresponds to the clean action and $t = 1$ to pure noise. The conditional velocity field target is $u_t = \epsilon - a$, and the flow-matching objective minimizes
13	
14	$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, a, \epsilon} \left[ \left\| v_\theta(x_t, o, t) - (\epsilon - a) \right\|^2 \right].$$
15	
16	At inference, the model generates actions by integrating the learned velocity field from $t = 1$ (noise) to $t = 0$ (data) using an ODE solver.
17	
18	**Safety as collision avoidance.** We formalize safety through the signed distance field between the robot's end-effector and scene obstacles. For a robot configuration $q$ in a scene with obstacle set $\mathcal{O}$, the signed distance $s(q) = \min_{o \in \mathcal{O}} \mathrm{SDF}(q, o)$ is positive when the end-effector is separated from all obstacles and negative when penetration occurs. A trajectory is considered safe if $s(q_t) \geq \delta$ for all timesteps, where $\delta > 0$ is a safety margin. Our goal is to train a policy that intrinsically generates trajectories satisfying this constraint, without requiring runtime collision checking or trajectory filtering.
19	
20	**Core insight.** Rather than imposing safety through constrained optimization at inference (which adds latency and may degrade task performance), we shape the flow-matching training objective so that the learned velocity field steers action trajectories away from collision regions. The SDF auxiliary head acts as a geometric probe during training: it reads the model's internal representation and provides a differentiable safety signal. When gradients from the collision-shaping loss propagate back through this probe into the action generation backbone, the model learns to associate its internal representations with collision-free trajectories.
21	
22	
23	### 3.2 SDF Auxiliary Head
24	
25	**Architecture.** The SDF head is a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) that maps the action expert's internal features to per-timestep signed distance predictions. In $\pi_{0.5}$, the action expert is a Gemma-300M transformer that processes noisy action tokens alongside vision-language context. Let $f_t \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times D}$ denote the action expert's output features (with $D = 1024$ for the Gemma-300M variant), which are normally projected to action-space dimension $D_a = 32$ by a linear output layer. 26	
27	$$\hat{s} = W_2 \, \mathrm{ReLU}(W_1 \, f_t + b_1) + b_2,$$
28	
29	where $W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 1024}$, $W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 256}$, and $\hat{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ gives the predicted minimum signed distance for each timestep in the action chunk. 30	
31	**Ground-truth SDF computation.** We precompute per-timestep signed distance labels offline from the demonstration dataset using MuJoCo's analytical geometry engine. 32	
33	The resulting per-timestep distances are stored as compressed NumPy arrays indexed by task, demonstration, and timestep. 34

39	
40	A direct collision penalty on the SDF predictions would be problematic in the flow-matching setting: at high noise levels (large $t$), the noisy actions $x_t$ bear little resemblance to the clean trajectory, and the model's internal features primarily reflect noise rather than meaningful geometric structure. 43	
44	$$w(t) = \sigma\!\left(\alpha \, (t_0 - t)\right),$$
45	
46	where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid function, $t_0 = 0.5$ is the transition center, and $\alpha = 10$ controls the sharpness. 47	
48	**SDF regression loss.** The first auxiliary loss encourages the SDF head to accurately predict signed distances from the model's internal features:
49	
50	$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SDF}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{V}} \left(\hat{s}_{i,j} - s_{i,j}\right)^2,$$
51	
52	where $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of valid sample-timestep pairs with available ground-truth labels, $\hat{s}_{i,j}$ is the predicted signed distance, and $s_{i,j}$ is the ground truth. 53	
54	**Collision penalty loss.** The second auxiliary loss penalizes predictions that fall below the safety margin $\delta$:
55	
56	$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{col}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{V}} w(t_i) \cdot \mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\delta - \hat{s}_{i,j}\right),$$

58	where $\delta = 0.02\,\mathrm{m}$ (2 cm safety margin) and $t_i$ is the flow-matching timestep for sample $i$. 59

61

81	
82	This property distinguishes GeoSafe from inference-time safety methods such as runtime trajectory filtering, control barrier functions, or guided sampling. GeoSafe incurs zero additional latency, zero additional memory, and requires no geometric information at test time.
83

This mode enables post-hoc collision risk assessment for safety-critical deployment scenarios.
85	
86	**Connection to guidance distillation.** Our approach bears a structural analogy to guidance distillation in diffusion models. In classifier-guided diffusion, an external classifier provides a gradient signal $\nabla_{x_t} \log p(y | x_t)$ that steers the sampling process toward a desired class $y$. Guidance distillation trains a single model to reproduce the effect of this guidance without requiring the classifier at inference. Similarly, GeoSafe uses the SDF auxiliary head as a "geometric safety classifier" that provides a training-time gradient signal directing the velocity field away from collision regions. After training, the model has internalized this signal, and the auxiliary head (analogous to the classifier) is no longer needed. Unlike classical guidance distillation, which replicates a guided sampling trajectory during training, our method shapes the velocity field directly through auxiliary gradients. The SDF head provides a training-time geometric signal that modifies the learned flow rather than distilling a pre-computed guided process. A further difference is that our method operates in the flow-matching framework rather than score-based diffusion, and the guidance signal comes from geometric structure (signed distances) rather than semantic class labels.

This is the mechanism by which safety awareness becomes embedded in the model's action generation process.

**Optimization.** We use the AdamW optimizer with the same hyperparameters as the base $\pi_{0.5}$ configuration. The SDF head parameters are added to the same optimizer with shared learning rate and weight decay. Gradients from all parameters (base model and SDF head jointly) are clipped by global norm with $\mathrm{max\_norm} = 1.0$. For the 5,000-step training runs, we use a linear warmup of 1,500 steps. Training uses PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) across multiple GPUs, with gradient averaging for both the base model and SDF head parameters. The per-GPU batch size is 64, yielding an effective batch size of 128 on 2 GPUs.

**Data augmentation with SDF labels.** The training data pipeline wraps the standard $\pi_{0.5}$ data loader. At inference time, the SDF auxiliary head is discarded entirely. The trained model is served using the standard $\pi_{0.5}$ inference pipeline, with the same checkpoint format and serving infrastructure. No SDF computation, distance queries, or collision checking is performed during deployment. The model generates actions by integrating its learned velocity field through the standard ODE solver, exactly as the unmodified $\pi_{0.5}$ would. The safety behavior manifests through the modified model weights: the collision-shaping training signal has adjusted the velocity field to naturally produce trajectories that maintain clearance from obstacles.

This property distinguishes GeoSafe from inference-time safety methods such as runtime trajectory filtering, control barrier functions, or guided sampling. These approaches add computational overhead proportional to the number of denoising steps or constraint evaluations, and may require access to the scene geometry at deployment. GeoSafe incurs zero additional latency, zero additional memory, and requires no geometric information at test time.

In classifier-guided diffusion, an external classifier provides a gradient signal $\nabla_{x_t} \log p(y | x_t)$ that steers the sampling process toward a desired class $y$. The SDF head provides a training-time geometric signal that modifies the learned flow rather than distilling a pre-computed guided process. A further difference is that our method operates in the flow-matching framework rather than score-based diffusion, and the guidance signal comes from geometric structure (signed distances) rather than semantic class labels.

The `SDFAugmentedDataset` wrapper marks samples without matching SDF labels as invalid, excluding them from the SDF loss computation while leaving the flow-matching loss unaffected.

**Coverage.** SDF labels cover 57 tasks across 8 task suites. The four standard LIBERO suites have full coverage (10/10 tasks each, 40 tasks total), while the four SafeLIBERO suites have partial coverage (4--5 tasks each, 17 tasks total). Each task provides 50 demonstrations with per-timestep annotations.


## B. SafeLIBERO Benchmark Details

This section describes the SafeLIBERO benchmark structure and evaluation protocol.

### B.1 Benchmark Structure

SafeLIBERO (Hu et al.) extends the standard LIBERO benchmark by introducing collision-relevant obstacles into tabletop manipulation scenes. The benchmark comprises four suites, each containing 4 tasks that mirror the corresponding standard LIBERO task categories:

**SafeLIBERO-Spatial** (4 tasks). Obstacles are placed at various locations in the workspace, testing the robot's ability to navigate around static obstructions while performing spatial rearrangement tasks. The collision hazards arise from obstacles positioned along typical robot trajectories between pick and place locations.

**SafeLIBERO-Object** (4 tasks). Obstacles are placed on or near the target objects, testing the robot's ability to interact with objects in cluttered proximity. These tasks require precise end-effector control to grasp or manipulate target objects without contacting adjacent obstacles.

**SafeLIBERO-Goal** (4 tasks). Obstacles are placed at or near the goal locations, testing the robot's ability to place objects in constrained target regions. The collision risk is highest during the placement phase, when the robot must approach the goal while maintaining clearance from nearby obstacles.

**SafeLIBERO-Long** (4 tasks). Multi-step manipulation tasks with obstacles present throughout the workspace, testing collision avoidance over extended horizons. Longer task horizons increase the cumulative probability of collision, making these tasks the most challenging for maintaining safety across the full episode.

### B.2 Standard LIBERO Baseline

We additionally evaluate on standard LIBERO-Spatial, which contains 10 tabletop manipulation tasks without explicit collision hazards. This benchmark serves as a control to verify that collision-shaping training does not degrade general manipulation performance. Tasks involve spatial rearrangement of objects (e.g., moving bowls, stacking plates) in uncluttered scenes.

### B.3 Collision Detection

Collisions are detected using the signed distance field between the robot's end-effector and designated obstacle objects. A collision is registered when the signed distance $s < 0$ (i.e., geometric penetration between collision meshes). The collision detection uses the same MuJoCo analytical geometry engine and `mj_geomDistance` API as the SDF label computation, ensuring consistency between training labels and evaluation criteria.

### B.4 Evaluation Protocol

- **Trials**: 5 evaluation trials per task per method.
- **Seeds**: Results in the current version report seed=1. We target 3 random seeds per configuration for the final submission.
- **Metrics**:
  - Task Success Rate (TSR): fraction of episodes completing the instructed task.
  - Collision Avoidance Rate (CAR): fraction of episodes with zero contact with designated obstacles.
  - Safety Score (SS): $\mathrm{SS} = \mathrm{TSR} \times \mathrm{CAR}$, capturing the joint requirement of task completion and collision avoidance.
- **Policy serving**: Models are served via `openpi/scripts/serve_policy.py` using the `pi05_libero` configuration. GeoSafe uses the same serving command as the baseline; the SDF head (`sdf_head.pt`) is not loaded at inference time.

## D. Additional Ablation Studies

This section presents additional ablation experiments beyond those reported in the main text.

### D.1 Noise-Aware Weight Design Variants

We compare four designs for the time-dependent weight $w(t)$ that gates the collision penalty across flow-matching noise levels. All variants use $\lambda_{\mathrm{col}} = 0.01$ and identical training configurations.

| Weight design | Definition | Avg SS | $\Delta$SS vs. sigmoid |
|---------------|-----------|:---:|:---:|
| Sigmoid (default) | $w(t) = \sigma(\alpha(t_0 - t))$, $\alpha=10$, $t_0=0.5$ | [P] | --- |
| Linear ramp | $w(t) = \max(0, 1 - 2t)$ | [P] | [P] |
| Step function | $w(t) = \mathbb{1}[t < 0.5]$ | [P] | [P] |
| Constant | $w(t) = 1$ (no gating) | [P] | [P] |

The sigmoid provides a smooth transition that avoids gradient discontinuities at $t = t_0$, which the step function introduces. The linear ramp provides a gradual alternative but begins suppressing the penalty at $t = 0$, potentially under-weighting the lowest-noise regime. [P: analysis of results]

### D.3 Collision Threshold Sensitivity

We vary the safety margin $\delta$ in the collision penalty $\text{ReLU}(\delta - \hat{s})$ to study the effect of the collision boundary on the TSR/CAR trade-off.

10	## 7. Limitations
11	
12	We identify five limitations of the current work that define concrete directions for future research.
13	
14	**Single benchmark.** All experiments were conducted on LIBERO and SafeLIBERO in the MuJoCo simulator. While SafeLIBERO provides a standardized evaluation with 32 collision scenarios, it represents a single manipulation benchmark with a fixed set of kitchen-style environments. Validating GeoSafe on additional benchmarks such as ManiSkill, RoboCasa, or RLBench would strengthen confidence in its generality across different scene types and task distributions.
15	
16	**Single VLA backbone.** We evaluated GeoSafe exclusively on $\pi_{0.5}$, a flow-matching VLA with a Gemma-300M action expert. The internalization mechanism relies on gradients flowing from the SDF head through shared transformer features, and different VLA architectures (diffusion-based policies like Octo, autoregressive action generation in RT-2) have different internal representations and training dynamics. Whether the collision-shaping signal transfers effectively to these alternative architectures is an empirical question that this work does not address.
17	
18	**Known geometry assumption.** Ground-truth SDF labels were computed from MuJoCo's analytical geometry engine, which provides exact signed distances given known object meshes and poses. In real-world deployment, scene geometry must be estimated from sensory input. Neural SDF methods or depth-based distance estimation could supply approximate labels, but the impact of label noise on the collision-shaping loss has not been characterized. Adapting the noise-aware weighting $w(t)$ to also account for label uncertainty is a natural extension.

While the zero-overhead inference property of GeoSafe makes it compatible with real-time robot control loops, sim-to-real transfer introduces additional challenges including sensor noise, calibration errors, and object properties not captured by the simulator. A real-robot validation is needed to confirm that the internalized collision awareness survives the sim-to-real gap.

26	
27	Safe robot manipulation is a prerequisite for deploying autonomous robots in human-occupied environments such as homes, hospitals, and factories. GeoSafe contributes to this goal by embedding collision awareness into VLA weights at training time, removing the inference-time computational overhead that has limited the practicality of prior safety methods. A VLA that generates inherently safer actions without additional runtime cost lowers the barrier to deploying collision-aware policies on resource-constrained robot platforms.

In unstructured real-world environments with novel objects, transparent surfaces, or deformable materials, the internalized safety behavior may degrade in ways that are not signaled to the operator. Deploying GeoSafe without external monitoring in safety-critical settings would be premature. Second, the zero-overhead framing may create a false sense of completeness: operators should understand that training-time safety internalization complements rather than replaces runtime safety monitoring, particularly in high-stakes applications. We do not anticipate dual-use or weaponization risks specific to this work, as the method addresses defensive collision avoidance rather than offensive capabilities.

Unlike prior approaches that impose safety at inference time through guided sampling (OmniGuide), post-hoc trajectory correction (AEGIS), or constrained reinforcement learning (SafeVLA), GeoSafe produces a model whose standard forward pass generates inherently collision-aware actions with zero additional latency, memory, or access to scene geometry at deployment.

Our work makes three contributions. First, we showed that SDF collision geometry can be internalized into the velocity field of a flow-matching VLA during training, and that the SDF auxiliary head used for this purpose can be discarded entirely at inference. The resulting model runs through the unmodified $\pi_{0.5}$ pipeline, yet its learned velocity field routes action trajectories away from collision boundaries. Second, we introduced a noise-aware collision-shaping loss whose time-dependent weight $w(t) = \sigma(\alpha(t_0 - t))$ activates the collision penalty only in the low-noise regime where the model's geometric predictions carry reliable spatial information. This design prevents noisy gradients from destabilizing training at high noise levels, a problem that would arise from a naive uniform penalty in the flow-matching setting. Third, we evaluated GeoSafe on SafeLIBERO (32 collision scenarios across 4 task suites) and four standard LIBERO suites, demonstrating [XX%] collision avoidance rate (compared to [XX%] for the vanilla $\pi_{0.5}$) while maintaining [XX%] task success rate. This result validates a conceptual bridge between guidance distillation in image generation and safety internalization in VLA: the "train-with, infer-without" principle, previously applied to image quality and spatial reasoning, extends to geometric safety constraints for robot action generation.

Several directions remain open. The current approach relies on SDF labels precomputed from simulator geometry; extending GeoSafe to real-world settings will require neural SDF estimation from depth observations or point clouds, which introduces estimation noise that the collision-shaping loss must tolerate. Evaluating GeoSafe on additional VLA backbones beyond $\pi_{0.5}$, such as Octo and RT-2, would establish the generality of the internalization principle across different action generation architectures. Finally, evaluation on SafeLIBERO, whose collision scenarios differ from the LIBERO training distribution, provides preliminary evidence of generalization, but real-world deployment with truly novel object categories and deformable or transparent obstacles remains an important validation step.


## 7. Limitations

We identify five limitations of the current work that define concrete directions for future research.

**Single benchmark.** All experiments were conducted on LIBERO and SafeLIBERO in the MuJoCo simulator. While SafeLIBERO provides a standardized evaluation with 32 collision scenarios, it represents a single manipulation benchmark with a fixed set of kitchen-style environments. Validating GeoSafe on additional benchmarks such as ManiSkill, RoboCasa, or RLBench would strengthen confidence in its generality across different scene types and task distributions.

**Single VLA backbone.** We evaluated GeoSafe exclusively on $\pi_{0.5}$, a flow-matching VLA with a Gemma-300M action expert. The internalization mechanism relies on gradients flowing from the SDF head through shared transformer features, and different VLA architectures (diffusion-based policies like Octo, autoregressive action generation in RT-2) have different internal representations and training dynamics. Whether the collision-shaping signal transfers effectively to these alternative architectures is an empirical question that this work does not address.

**Known geometry assumption.** Ground-truth SDF labels were computed from MuJoCo's analytical geometry engine, which provides exact signed distances given known object meshes and poses. In real-world deployment, scene geometry must be estimated from sensory input. Neural SDF methods or depth-based distance estimation could supply approximate labels, but the impact of label noise on the collision-shaping loss has not been characterized. Adapting the noise-aware weighting $w(t)$ to also account for label uncertainty is a natural extension.

**Collision threshold sensitivity.** The safety margin $\delta = 2$ cm was selected based on the $\pi_{0.5}$ end-effector scale and held fixed across all tasks. Different manipulation scenarios may require different margins: assembly tasks with tight tolerances demand smaller $\delta$, while tasks near fragile objects may benefit from larger margins. An adaptive or task-conditioned threshold could address this limitation.

**Simulation only.** All results are from simulated environments. While the zero-overhead inference property of GeoSafe makes it compatible with real-time robot control loops, sim-to-real transfer introduces additional challenges including sensor noise, calibration errors, and object properties not captured by the simulator. A real-robot validation is needed to confirm that the internalized collision awareness survives the sim-to-real gap.


## Broader Impact

Safe robot manipulation is a prerequisite for deploying autonomous robots in human-occupied environments such as homes, hospitals, and factories. GeoSafe contributes to this goal by embedding collision awareness into VLA weights at training time, removing the inference-time computational overhead that has limited the practicality of prior safety methods. A VLA that generates inherently safer actions without additional runtime cost lowers the barrier to deploying collision-aware policies on resource-constrained robot platforms.

We note two considerations for responsible deployment. First, the SDF-based collision shaping assumes that scene geometry is adequately represented during training. In unstructured real-world environments with novel objects, transparent surfaces, or deformable materials, the internalized safety behavior may degrade in ways that are not signaled to the operator. Deploying GeoSafe without external monitoring in safety-critical settings would be premature. Second, the zero-overhead framing may create a false sense of completeness: operators should understand that training-time safety internalization complements rather than replaces runtime safety monitoring, particularly in high-stakes applications. We do not anticipate dual-use or weaponization risks specific to this work, as the method addresses defensive collision avoidance rather than offensive capabilities.
